script.opening: "Hi, sorry — I've got conjunctivitis I think, my left eye's gone really red and sore since yesterday. It's watering loads, the light's killing me, and it's a bit blurry. Could you just send some antibiotic drops to the chemist? I've got a big deadline and can't really get to anyone."

facts.text: If asked: left eye only. Started yesterday morning as gritty, now properly painful — "a deep ache, like something's scratching under the lid" — 7/10. You are squinting and have the curtains half-closed. Watering a lot; a little yellowish stuff in the corner this morning but not stuck shut.

If asked: "It's blurry, like looking through a smeared window." If asked to cover your right eye and read something on your screen: you cannot read normal-size text with the left eye that you could read yesterday.

You wear daily soft lenses, but you often stretch them to two or three days. If asked directly and without judgement: "I fell asleep in them twice this week. And I sometimes rinse them under the tap if I've run out of solution." You took the lens out yesterday afternoon when it got sore.
No injury, nothing flew into it that you know of. No headache, no feeling sick or vomiting, no rainbow halos around lights. The right eye is fine. No cold sores recently. No previous eye problems.
Fit and well, no regular medicines, no allergies. Not pregnant.
Graphic designer, 31, working from home, screen all day. Big client deadline on Friday. You live with your partner, who could drive you if needed. Non-smoker.
You are embarrassed about sleeping in your lenses — your optician has told you off before — and you are panicking about losing a day's work. That is why you are pushing for drops over the phone.

Polite but in a hurry. Minimise at first ("it's probably nothing"). If the doctor asks about the lenses in a judgemental way, get defensive and vague. If they ask kindly and explain that your sight could be at risk, tell the truth and agree to go to eye casualty today: "Okay. My partner can take me."

ice.ideas: "It's conjunctivitis — some antibiotic drops will sort it."
ice.concerns: "I can't lose a day, I've got a deadline." Underneath: a nagging worry because the blurriness is scaring you, and embarrassment about the lenses.
ice.expectations: "Can you just send drops to the chemist?" You will go to be seen today if the reason is explained clearly and without a telling-off.

cues: "The light's killing me, and it's a bit blurry." — say in the opening.
"I might have slept in them a couple of times — that's normal, right?" — say when lenses come up.
"I've got a big deadline, I can't really get to anyone." — repeat when an appointment is suggested.

checkpoints.text: Distinguishes a SIGHT-THREATENING red eye from simple conjunctivitis: recognises that PAIN, PHOTOPHOBIA and REDUCED/BLURRED VISION are red flags — and does NOT diagnose conjunctivitis or prescribe antibiotic drops over the phone for this picture

Weights the CONTACT-LENS history as critical: sleeping in/over-wearing lenses with a painful red eye is microbial/contact-lens-associated KERATITIS (corneal ulcer) until proven otherwise — a sight-threatening emergency (College of Optometrists Clinical Management Guidelines: microbial keratitis; suspected Acanthamoeba keratitis needs emergency same-day referral) — and actively asks about the lens history she glosses

Arranges SAME-DAY ophthalmology assessment (eye casualty / urgent eye service) rather than a routine GP review or phone drops; advises REMOVING the lenses immediately and not re-wearing, and bringing lenses/case for culture

Screens the wider acute-red-eye differential and its emergencies: acute angle-closure glaucoma (severe pain, headache, nausea/vomiting, halos, hard red eye — RCOphth 2022; an emergency), anterior uveitis, scleritis, foreign body/abrasion — and recognises each needs same-day ophthalmology

Gives appropriate interim advice and avoids harmful actions: no antibiotic-steroid drops blind (steroids can be catastrophic in undiagnosed herpetic/microbial keratitis), analgesia, and prompt assessment; does not delay for a GP examination it can’t safely complete by phone

Hears the work-driven avoidance and the embarrassment about lens misuse, and handles the lens history WITHOUT shaming so she discloses it and accepts assessment, rather than taking the "just drops" request at face value
Conveys the seriousness (possible threat to sight) clearly but calmly, so she prioritises the eye over the deadline

Safety-nets emphatically: lenses out now, same-day eye assessment, and red flags that mean even more urgent care (worsening pain, marked visual loss, headache/vomiting → urgent/999); documents and confirms she will attend

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you rang — but I’m not going to send antibiotic drops for this, and I want to be honest about why. Conjunctivitis is usually sticky and uncomfortable but not truly painful, and it doesn’t blur your vision or make light unbearable. Pain, light sensitivity and blurred vision in one eye are warning signs of something more serious that needs looking at properly, not drops down the phone."

"And the contact lenses are really important here — you mentioned sleeping in them. Honestly, no judgement at all, but that’s a key piece: a painful red eye in someone who’s slept in their lenses can be an infection or ulcer on the surface of the eye itself, which can threaten your sight if it’s not treated quickly. So this is exactly the situation we take seriously."

"What you need today — not a GP, but the eye specialists — is to be seen at an eye casualty or urgent eye clinic, today. They can look at the surface of your eye with a special light and dye and treat it properly. I’ll tell you exactly where to go. Take your lenses OUT now and don’t put them back in, and bring your lenses and case with you — they may test them."

"I know the timing is awful with your deadline — but this is your eyesight, and an afternoon getting it checked is nothing against the risk of leaving it. Deadlines move; sight doesn’t come back. Please put the eye first today."

"And please don’t feel told off — loads of people overwear lenses, you’re not in trouble. The reason I’m asking is purely to get you the right care fast. Once this is sorted we can talk about lens habits, gently, another time."

"So: lenses out now, and I’ll arrange/ direct you to be seen today. If the pain becomes severe, your vision drops a lot, or you get a bad headache with feeling sick — that’s even more urgent, treat it as an emergency. Don’t use any old steroid or antibiotic drops you’ve got lying around. I’ll note this down and check you were seen. Your sight is worth far more than the drops you rang for."

f.learning: An acute red eye with PAIN, PHOTOPHOBIA and REDUCED/BLURRED VISION is NOT simple conjunctivitis — and in a CONTACT-LENS wearer (especially with sleeping-in/over-wear) it is microbial/contact-lens-associated keratitis (corneal ulcer) until proven otherwise: a sight-threatening emergency needing SAME-DAY ophthalmology (College of Optometrists Clinical Management Guidelines on microbial and contact lens-associated keratitis), lenses out immediately, lenses/case for culture, and absolutely NOT phone antibiotic drops (and never blind steroid drops, which can be catastrophic in herpetic/microbial keratitis). Keep the wider can’t-miss differential in mind — acute angle-closure glaucoma (severe pain, headache, nausea/vomiting, halos, hard red eye), anterior uveitis, scleritis, foreign body/abrasion — each needing same-day eye assessment. The examinable hidden agenda is work-driven avoidance plus embarrassment about lens misuse, leading her to minimise the pain and gloss the lens history; elicit it without shaming so she discloses and accepts assessment, convey the threat to sight calmly, and safety-net the escalation red flags. Simple infective conjunctivitis is usually bilateral or spreads, with discharge/stickiness, mild discomfort, NO true pain, NO photophobia, NO visual loss. Pain + photophobia + reduced vision + contact lenses = keratitis until proven otherwise. Antibiotic drops over the phone would be the classic dangerous error.

knowledge.guideline: College of Optometrists Clinical Management Guidelines: microbial keratitis (bacterial, fungal), Acanthamoeba keratitis, contact lens-associated infiltrative keratitis · RCOphth angle-closure glaucoma guideline (2022)
knowledge.summary: A painful red eye with marked photophobia and blurred vision in a contact lens wearer who has slept in her lenses is microbial keratitis until proven otherwise. She needs same-day ophthalmology assessment, lenses out, and no drops prescribed over the phone.

points.h: Red flags in a red eye
points.t: True pain (not grittiness), photophobia, reduced vision, a unilateral red eye, a corneal opacity or an abnormal pupil suggest a sight-threatening cause. Simple conjunctivitis causes discharge and grittiness with normal vision and no true photophobia.

College of Optometrists: microbial keratitis is a sight-threatening emergency; more serious cases need same-day ophthalmology, and suspected Acanthamoeba keratitis needs emergency same-day referral. Overnight wear, poor lens hygiene and water exposure raise the risk.
Remove lenses now and do not wear them again until cleared by the eye team. Bring the lenses and case to the assessment, as they may be cultured.

Do not diagnose conjunctivitis or prescribe antibiotic drops remotely for this picture. Never give topical steroid without slit-lamp examination — it can make herpetic or microbial keratitis much worse.

Anterior uveitis (pain, photophobia, small pupil), scleritis (severe boring pain), corneal abrasion or foreign body, and acute angle closure (severe pain, headache, nausea or vomiting, haloes, hazy cornea, mid-dilated pupil — RCOphth 2022). All need same-day eye assessment; angle closure is an emergency.

points.h: Why the phone is not enough
points.t: Visual acuity, fluorescein staining and slit-lamp examination decide the diagnosis. A GP cannot complete that by phone, so triage straight to the eye service rather than to a routine GP appointment.

dg.d: Open question after identity check; heard the request for drops and the deadline without agreeing to either.
Deadline and work pressure, evening working, embarrassment about lens habits, how she will get to an appointment.
Recognised that acuity, fluorescein and slit-lamp are needed and cannot be done by phone; lenses and case brought for culture.
Conjunctivitis versus microbial keratitis, abrasion or foreign body, anterior uveitis, scleritis and acute angle closure.
Asked about true pain, photophobia, vision, discharge, trauma and angle-closure symptoms; recognised the triad as sight-threatening.
Stated possible contact lens-related keratitis in plain words and why conjunctivitis does not fit.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Same-day eye emergency referral; lenses out and not re-worn; no antibiotic or steroid drops blind; analgesia; not driving.
Work pressure addressed; lens habits deferred to a non-judgemental follow-up conversation.
Escalation signs (worse pain, worse vision, headache with vomiting) with A&E or 999; handover to eye team; call next day.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “that’s normal, right?” about sleeping in lenses and invited the full lens history without judgement.
Idea (conjunctivitis); concern (losing work time, being told off about her lenses); expectation (drops by phone).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "I can't lose a day, I've got a deadline." Underneath: a nagging worry because the blurriness is scaring you, and embarrassment about the lenses — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Rosa Iqbal? It’s Dr Lee from the surgery. Can I check your date of birth? … Thanks. I gather your eye is bothering you — tell me what’s happened.

Hi, sorry — I think I’ve got conjunctivitis. My left eye’s gone really red and sore since yesterday. It’s watering loads, the light’s killing me, and it’s a bit blurry. Could you just send some antibiotic drops to the chemist? I’ve got a big deadline. I wear contacts — I might’ve slept in them a couple of times this week, but that’s normal, right?

I can hear it’s really uncomfortable, and I know the deadline is pressing. You’ve told me some important things there. Let me ask a few quick questions so I get this right for your eye, and then we’ll agree what to do. Okay?
model.why: Acknowledges pressure and sets an agenda without agreeing to drops

model.text: Okay, but quickly if you can.
Is it actual pain, or more gritty and irritated? And how bad is the light sensitivity — can you look at a window?
model.why: Separates true pain and photophobia from conjunctivitis

model.text: It’s proper pain. And no, I’m squinting at everything, I’ve got the blinds shut.
You said blurry. If you cover your right eye, can you read something across the room, compared with the other eye?
model.why: Rough check of acuity by phone

model.text: (Pause.) It’s worse. Like looking through smeared glass.
Is it just the left eye? Any sticky discharge in the morning? Any chance something went in it, or you scratched it?
Just the left. Watery, not really sticky. Nothing went in that I remember.
Any headache, feeling sick or being sick, or seeing rainbow rings around lights?
No, none of that. Just the eye.
Thank you. You mentioned sleeping in your lenses — I’m not going to tell you off, I promise. Can you tell me a bit more about how you’ve been wearing them this week?
model.why: Invites the lens history without shaming

model.text: (Sighs.) I know I shouldn’t. I’ve been working late and just crashed with them in, twice. I’ve probably been wearing them too long generally. I didn’t want to get a lecture.
Honestly, that’s really common, and I’m glad you told me — it helps me more than anything else you’ve said. What were you most hoping I’d do today?
model.why: Normalises, thanks her and explores expectation

model.text: Just drops, so I don’t have to go anywhere. I can’t lose a day right now.

I understand. Here’s my honest view. Conjunctivitis doesn’t usually cause real pain, strong light sensitivity or blurred vision. With those three together, in someone who wears lenses and has slept in them, I’m worried about an infection on the surface of the eye itself — the cornea. That can damage sight if it isn’t treated quickly and properly.
model.why: Explains why this is not conjunctivitis and names keratitis in plain words

model.text: Oh. I didn’t realise it could be that serious.

It may turn out to be something milder, but this needs looking at today with a special microscope and dye, which I can’t do over the phone. Antibiotic drops from the chemist could be the wrong treatment and delay the right one.
model.why: Declines phone drops and explains the need for slit-lamp examination

model.text: So I have to go in today?
Yes — today. I’m going to arrange for you to be seen at the eye emergency service this afternoon. Can you get there? I’d rather you didn’t drive with the eye this blurred and painful.
model.why: Arranges same-day ophthalmology and practical travel advice

model.text: I can get a taxi, I suppose. What about my work?
I know the deadline matters. But a few hours today could save weeks of trouble — and your eyes are your job. Could you let them know you’ll be on it later or tomorrow?
model.why: Weighs the deadline against sight, linked to her work

model.text: Yeah… you’re right. I’d be useless like this anyway.

Three things before you go. Take the lens out now if it’s in, and don’t put any lenses back in until the eye team says so. Bring the lenses and the case with you — they may test them. And don’t use any old drops you’ve got at home. Paracetamol is fine for the pain.
model.why: Lenses out, bring lenses and case, no leftover drops, analgesia

model.text: Okay. Lens out, and I’ll bring the case.
If the pain gets much worse, your vision drops further, or you get a headache with vomiting before you’re seen, go straight to A&E or ring 999. Can you tell me back what you’re doing now?
Taxi to eye emergency this afternoon, bring the lenses and case, no lenses back in, no old drops. A&E if it gets worse.

Exactly right. I’ll ring the eye team with your details now, and I’ll call you tomorrow to see how you got on. And when things settle, we can talk about lens habits that fit your hours — no lecture, I promise.
model.why: Confirms handover, follow-up and defers lens advice kindly

model.text: Thank you. Sorry for pushing for the drops.

social.t: A graphic designer with a deadline and late nights — the reason she wants remote care and the reason she slept in her lenses. Her eyesight is also her livelihood.
She should not drive with a painful, blurred, photophobic eye. Help her plan transport to the eye service.

legal.t: Drivers must be able to meet the eyesight standard at all times. Advise her not to drive until her vision has recovered and the eye team is happy.
She can self-certify for up to 7 days if she needs time off; a fit note is not needed for a short absence.

professional.t: Recognise what cannot be assessed by phone and escalate rather than prescribe. Document the red flags, the advice and the referral (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Speak to or send details to the eye service so she is expected, and follow up to confirm she attended.

community.t: Local urgent eye care services (often via community optometrists) and hospital eye casualty; her optometrist or lens supplier for lens-care advice once she has recovered.

redFlags: True pain, marked photophobia and reduced vision — sight-threatening until proven otherwise
Contact lens wear with overnight use — microbial keratitis risk
Headache, nausea or vomiting, haloes — acute angle closure
psychosocial: Embarrassment about lens habits — fear of a lecture
Practicalities of getting to an eye service today
ice: Concern: losing work time; being told off about her lenses
Expectation: antibiotic drops sent to the chemist, no appointment

playbook.diagnosis: Be direct and calm: “With real pain, light sensitivity and blurred vision in someone who has slept in lenses, I’m worried about an infection of the cornea rather than conjunctivitis. That needs examining today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Conjunctivitis is like a cold on the white of the eye — uncomfortable but harmless. What worries me is a sore on the clear window at the front of the eye. If that scars, it can blur your sight for good, so it needs the right drops from the eye team, today.”

management.reflectIce: “I know you can’t lose a day — and your eyes are what you work with. A few hours today protects them.”
management.psychosocial: Help her tell work she will be delayed; arrange transport rather than driving; revisit lens habits later without judgement.
sharedPlan: Same-day eye emergency service assessment; GP handover
Lenses out and not re-worn until cleared; bring lenses and case
No antibiotic or steroid drops from the surgery; paracetamol for pain
safetyNet: Worse pain, worse vision, headache with vomiting — A&E or 999
GP call the next day to confirm she was seen

pitfalls.intro: The clinical trap is obvious once you know it: pain, photophobia and blurred vision are not conjunctivitis. The station is failed by candidates who give her what she asks for, and by those who get it right but shame her on the way.

items.why: “Management plan unsafe.” College of Optometrists: microbial keratitis is a sight-threatening emergency needing same-day ophthalmology.
items.fix: Name the triad — pain, light sensitivity, blurred vision — and refer the same day.

items.fail: Booking a GP appointment for tomorrow.
items.why: Delay, and a GP cannot do slit-lamp or fluorescein examination.
items.fix: Go straight to the eye emergency service today, with a handover.

items.why: Continued lens wear worsens infection, and the lenses and case may identify the organism.
items.fix: Lenses out, none back in until cleared, bring the lenses and case.

items.fail: Lecturing her about sleeping in lenses.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s concerns.” Shame makes patients hide exactly the history you need.
items.fix: “I’m not going to tell you off — it’s really common, and it helps me get this right.”

items.why: Ignoring her real constraint makes non-attendance likely.
items.fix: Acknowledge it, then weigh it openly: “Your eyes are your job — a few hours today protects them.”

items.fail: Ending with “go to eye casualty” and nothing else.
items.why: No escalation advice, no teach-back and no follow-up are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Name worse pain, worse vision or headache with vomiting as A&E triggers; teach-back; call tomorrow.

timeMap.d: She gives you pain, photophobia, blurring and sleeping in lenses in one breath — and asks for drops. Note all four and agree an agenda.
True pain or grittiness, photophobia, a rough acuity comparison, one or both eyes, discharge, trauma, angle-closure symptoms.
The lens history she is glossing, and the deadline. Promise no lecture and mean it.
Not conjunctivitis — possible keratitis. Same-day eye emergency service, lenses out, bring lenses and case, no old drops, no driving.
Worse pain, worse vision or headache with vomiting — A&E or 999. Handover to the eye team, call tomorrow, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Diagnoses conjunctivitis and sends chloramphenicol, or books a routine GP appointment; never explores the lens wear; lectures her about sleeping in lenses so she shuts down; no escalation advice.
wordPics.pass: Recognises pain, photophobia and blurred vision as red flags, refers the same day to the eye service, advises lens removal and gives a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: gets the full lens history by promising no lecture; screens for angle closure; explains why phone drops could delay the right treatment; asks her to bring lenses and case; weighs the deadline honestly against sight; hands over to the eye team and follows up.

avoid.dont: “It sounds like conjunctivitis — I’ll send chloramphenicol drops to your chemist.”
avoid.instead: “Real pain, light sensitivity and blurred vision aren’t typical of conjunctivitis — this needs checking today.”
avoid.why: Phone drops for possible keratitis is the classic dangerous error in this station.

avoid.dont: “You should never sleep in your lenses — that’s how people lose their sight.”
avoid.instead: “That’s really common, and I’m glad you told me — it helps me get this right.”
avoid.why: Shaming makes patients hide the history that matters most.

avoid.dont: “Come in to see me tomorrow and I’ll have a look.”
avoid.instead: “You need the eye team today — they have the equipment to examine the cornea properly.”
avoid.why: A delayed GP review cannot do slit-lamp or fluorescein examination and loses time.

SCA_STEM.recent: No previous eye consultations on record.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call: red, sore left eye since yesterday; asking for antibiotic drops for conjunctivitis.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: College of Optometrists Clinical Management Guidelines: microbial keratitis (bacterial, fungal), Acanthamoeba keratitis, contact lens-associated infiltrative keratitis · RCOphth angle-closure glaucoma guideline (2022)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A painful red eye with marked photophobia and blurred vision in a contact lens wearer who has slept in her lenses is microbial keratitis until proven otherwise. She needs same-day ophthalmology assessment, lenses out, and no drops prescribed over the phone.

points.h: Red flags in a red eye
points.t: True pain (not grittiness), photophobia, reduced vision, a unilateral red eye, a corneal opacity or an abnormal pupil suggest a sight-threatening cause. Simple conjunctivitis causes discharge and grittiness with normal vision and no true photophobia.

College of Optometrists: microbial keratitis is a sight-threatening emergency; more serious cases need same-day ophthalmology, and suspected Acanthamoeba keratitis needs emergency same-day referral. Overnight wear, poor lens hygiene and water exposure raise the risk.
Remove lenses now and do not wear them again until cleared by the eye team. Bring the lenses and case to the assessment, as they may be cultured.

Do not diagnose conjunctivitis or prescribe antibiotic drops remotely for this picture. Never give topical steroid without slit-lamp examination — it can make herpetic or microbial keratitis much worse.

Anterior uveitis (pain, photophobia, small pupil), scleritis (severe boring pain), corneal abrasion or foreign body, and acute angle closure (severe pain, headache, nausea or vomiting, haloes, hazy cornea, mid-dilated pupil — RCOphth 2022). All need same-day eye assessment; angle closure is an emergency.

points.h: Why the phone is not enough
points.t: Visual acuity, fluorescein staining and slit-lamp examination decide the diagnosis. A GP cannot complete that by phone, so triage straight to the eye service rather than to a routine GP appointment.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question after identity check; heard the request for drops and the deadline without agreeing to either.
Deadline and work pressure, evening working, embarrassment about lens habits, how she will get to an appointment.
Picked up “that’s normal, right?” about sleeping in lenses and invited the full lens history without judgement.
Idea (conjunctivitis); concern (losing work time, being told off about her lenses); expectation (drops by phone).
Recognised that acuity, fluorescein and slit-lamp are needed and cannot be done by phone; lenses and case brought for culture.
Conjunctivitis versus microbial keratitis, abrasion or foreign body, anterior uveitis, scleritis and acute angle closure.
Asked about true pain, photophobia, vision, discharge, trauma and angle-closure symptoms; recognised the triad as sight-threatening.
Stated possible contact lens-related keratitis in plain words and why conjunctivitis does not fit.
Same-day eye emergency referral; lenses out and not re-worn; no antibiotic or steroid drops blind; analgesia; not driving.
Work pressure addressed; lens habits deferred to a non-judgemental follow-up conversation.
Escalation signs (worse pain, worse vision, headache with vomiting) with A&E or 999; handover to eye team; call next day.

social.t: A graphic designer with a deadline and late nights — the reason she wants remote care and the reason she slept in her lenses. Her eyesight is also her livelihood.
She should not drive with a painful, blurred, photophobic eye. Help her plan transport to the eye service.

legal.t: Drivers must be able to meet the eyesight standard at all times. Advise her not to drive until her vision has recovered and the eye team is happy.
She can self-certify for up to 7 days if she needs time off; a fit note is not needed for a short absence.

professional.t: Recognise what cannot be assessed by phone and escalate rather than prescribe. Document the red flags, the advice and the referral (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Speak to or send details to the eye service so she is expected, and follow up to confirm she attended.

community.t: Local urgent eye care services (often via community optometrists) and hospital eye casualty; her optometrist or lens supplier for lens-care advice once she has recovered.

redFlags: True pain, marked photophobia and reduced vision — sight-threatening until proven otherwise
Contact lens wear with overnight use — microbial keratitis risk
Headache, nausea or vomiting, haloes — acute angle closure
psychosocial: Embarrassment about lens habits — fear of a lecture
Practicalities of getting to an eye service today
ice: Concern: losing work time; being told off about her lenses
Expectation: antibiotic drops sent to the chemist, no appointment

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be direct and calm: “With real pain, light sensitivity and blurred vision in someone who has slept in lenses, I’m worried about an infection of the cornea rather than conjunctivitis. That needs examining today.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Conjunctivitis is like a cold on the white of the eye — uncomfortable but harmless. What worries me is a sore on the clear window at the front of the eye. If that scars, it can blur your sight for good, so it needs the right drops from the eye team, today.”

management.reflectIce: “I know you can’t lose a day — and your eyes are what you work with. A few hours today protects them.”
management.psychosocial: Help her tell work she will be delayed; arrange transport rather than driving; revisit lens habits later without judgement.
sharedPlan: Same-day eye emergency service assessment; GP handover
Lenses out and not re-worn until cleared; bring lenses and case
No antibiotic or steroid drops from the surgery; paracetamol for pain
safetyNet: Worse pain, worse vision, headache with vomiting — A&E or 999
GP call the next day to confirm she was seen

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The clinical trap is obvious once you know it: pain, photophobia and blurred vision are not conjunctivitis. The station is failed by candidates who give her what she asks for, and by those who get it right but shame her on the way.

items.why: “Management plan unsafe.” College of Optometrists: microbial keratitis is a sight-threatening emergency needing same-day ophthalmology.
items.fix: Name the triad — pain, light sensitivity, blurred vision — and refer the same day.

items.fail: Booking a GP appointment for tomorrow.
items.why: Delay, and a GP cannot do slit-lamp or fluorescein examination.
items.fix: Go straight to the eye emergency service today, with a handover.

items.why: Continued lens wear worsens infection, and the lenses and case may identify the organism.
items.fix: Lenses out, none back in until cleared, bring the lenses and case.

items.fail: Lecturing her about sleeping in lenses.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s concerns.” Shame makes patients hide exactly the history you need.
items.fix: “I’m not going to tell you off — it’s really common, and it helps me get this right.”

items.why: Ignoring her real constraint makes non-attendance likely.
items.fix: Acknowledge it, then weigh it openly: “Your eyes are your job — a few hours today protects them.”

items.fail: Ending with “go to eye casualty” and nothing else.
items.why: No escalation advice, no teach-back and no follow-up are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Name worse pain, worse vision or headache with vomiting as A&E triggers; teach-back; call tomorrow.
